items.title: When trust becomes risk: The dark side of AI-assisted financial decision-making
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in financial decision-making, raising questions about how users’ trust and perceptions of algorithmic bias relate to behavioural vulnerability. This study examines the relationships among perceived algorithmic bias, trust in AI, perceived decision-making error risk, and AI-assisted risk-taking tendency, while investigating the moderating role of perceived human oversight. Using survey data from 252 respondents analysed through partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), the findings show that perceived algorithmic bias is positively associated with perceived decision-making error risk but is not significantly associated with trust in AI. Trust in AI is positively associated with both perceived decision-making error risk and AI-assisted risk-taking tendency. Perceived decision-making error risk is also positively associated with AI-assisted risk-taking tendency and provides a significant indirect pathway linking perceived algorithmic bias to this tendency. However, the indirect pathway through trust in AI is not statistically supported. Although the interaction between perceived human oversight and perceived algorithmic bias is statistically significant, the conditional effects at low, mean, and high levels of perceived oversight are not significant. These findings challenge the assumption that trust in AI is uniformly beneficial and highlight the distinction between trust, perceived decision-making error risk, and AI-assisted risk-taking tendency. The study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of behavioural vulnerability in AI-assisted financial decision-making and underscores the importance of transparent AI-supported recommendations, critical user evaluation, and meaningful human review.

items.title: Which Matters More for Academic Performance: Motivation or Positive Thinking?
items.abstract: This study used a cross-sectional research design to examine how motivation and positive thinking, both separately and together, are related to academic performance. A total of 340 sixteen-year-old students were randomly selected from a secondary school in Selangor, Malaysia. Motivation was measured using the 16-item Motivation Assessment Questionnaire (MAQ), which covers four dimensions: intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, goal orientation and self-efficacy. Positive thinking was measured using the 12-item Positive Thinking Assessment Scale (PTAS), which covers three dimensions: optimism, resilience and self-affirmation. The results showed a strong positive relationship between motivation and positive thinking (ρ = .768, p < .001). Both motivation and positive thinking had significant positive relationships with academic performance (β = .413 and .435, respectively; p < .001). Together, they explained 63.5% of the differences in students’ academic performance. However, the difference between their two regression coefficients was not statistically significant (p = .820). Among the seven dimensions, only extrinsic motivation (β = .318, p < .005) and self-affirmation (β = .312, p < .001) had significant relationships with academic performance when all seven dimensions were examined together. The study also examined two mediation models (Positive Thinking → Motivation → Academic Performance and Motivation → Positive Thinking → Academic Performance). The indirect relationships for the two models were .317 and .334, respectively, and the difference between them was not statistically significant (p > .05). Overall, the findings do not show that either motivation or positive thinking is a stronger predictor or mediator than the other. Instead, both are related to academic performance and provide useful information that is partly shared and partly unique to each.

items.title: Who Is Forming Their Desires? A Chokmah-Based Model of Digital Wisdom for Discipling Generation Alpha in the Age of Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become integrated into the everyday learning experiences of Indonesian children and adolescents more rapidly than Christian education has developed a theological framework for understanding how these technologies shape learners. Existing approaches primarily treat AI as a tool to be used ethically, leaving its formative influence largely unexamined. This conceptual article examines who shapes the desires of Generation Alpha when generative AI functions as a digital liturgy and how Christian education can respond through spiritual formation and discipleship rather than merely enforcing rules. Employing a model-building conceptual research design, the study integrates a canonical theological interpretation of Proverbs, Job, and Ecclesiastes with a structured integrative review of scholarship on AI and learning, liturgical anthropology, and Indonesia's deep learning (pembelajaran mendalam) policy. The analysis identifies three potentially counter-formative desires reinforced by habitual AI use: the desire for effortless answers, the preference for seemingly authoritative discourse, and the pursuit of unearned self-presentation. In response, the article proposes the Chokmah-Based Digital Wisdom Model, in which the fear of the LORD (yir'at YHWH) reorients desires and establishes three formative dimensions: awareness coram Deo, discernment, and wisdom understood as the joyful art of living well. The model outlines a weigh–test–live discipleship cycle, developmentally differentiated indicators spanning primary school through Grade 10, and five empirically testable propositions.

items.title: Who Will Conduct Science? Researchers’ Expectations of AI Capabilities and the Future of Scientific Work
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI systems have demonstrated their potential to outperform humans in conducting research and in answering previously unsolved scientific problems. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing research independently, the question shifts from how researchers should use AI to how much human resources will be required in scientific research and where. We surveyed researchers worldwide about their perspectives on AI-driven scientific research, prompted by OpenAI’s bulk release of mathematical solutions in October 2026. We received over 4,000 responses from researchers across 126 countries and a wide range of disciplines. Most respondents (62%) expected AI systems to be capable of conducting research tasks independently within three years, although expectations regarding the quality of AI-generated research varied, with 41% anticipating quality comparable to or exceeding that of competent human researchers. Respondents generally supported allowing AI to assume most roles in scientific research (each with a minimum of 48%), mainly under human supervision. AI developments made one-third of respondents concerned about their own job security; mathematicians and statisticians anticipated the greatest effects on their research and careers (45%), and researchers in the humanities and arts the least (30%). Despite concerns about potential negative career consequences, respondents overwhelmingly (74%) expected AI-driven research to accelerate scientific progress. Although the limitations of this survey restrict the generalizability of its findings, the results offer an overview of how researchers across more than a hundred countries perceive rapid advances in AI. They also highlight the need to monitor AI’s impact on the scientific workforce and inform policies that support the sustainable integration of AI into scientific research.

items.title: Will AI Replace Juniors? How Task Complexity Reduces Automation Risk
items.abstract: How does task complexity shape firms' willingness to substitute entry-level labour with artificial intelligence (AI) tools? We study this question using a pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing industry. Managers are randomly assigned to consider a long lasting need for additional capacity involving either well-structured and standardised tasks, or more complex tasks that require professional judgement, contextual knowledge and independent problem-solving. Relative to standardised tasks, complex tasks reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale and increase the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Further, pre-treatment responses indicate that managers expect the availability of AI applications to reduce hiring of both entry-level employees and experienced workers, but significantly more strongly for entry-level workers.

items.title: Work design in digital platform labor: Development and validation of the Microworking Conditions Scale
items.abstract: In light of the rise of AI, microwork is becoming an increasingly important branch of the platform economy. This global labor market of individual workers who label data and moderate content supports the development of technological innovation. Little is known about their working conditions and how these conditions affect their well-being, however. This article presents three studies that outline the development of an integrative framework of working conditions in microwork, a complementary scale, and the validation of this scale. Based on current literature on microwork and guided by Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the Microworking Conditions Scale (MWCS) comprises 15 working conditions, nine adopted from existing frameworks (e.g., Work Autonomy) and six newly conceptualized (e.g., Availability Requirement). The measurement structure of the MWCS was confirmed by exploratory factor analyses ( n = 407) and confirmatory factor analysis ( n = 455). All 15 microworking conditions show convergent, discriminant, criterion, and predictive validity. The final scale consists of 45 items, three per microworking condition. The MWCS addresses the fragmented nature of the literature on microworking conditions and fills in gaps in the measurement of new working conditions emerging from microwork. The article further discusses the theoretical and practical implications, as well as directions for future research.

items.abstract: Проверка результатов искусственного интеллекта требует времени специалистов и увеличивает расходы инновационного проекта. Её сокращение оставляет часть ошибок без исправления. Цель исследования состоит в экономическом обосновании объёма проверки однородных вспомогательных операций с обратимыми последствиями ошибок. Материалом послужили исследования взаимодействия человека и алгоритма, организационной готовности и управления рисками. Применены аналитическое моделирование, сопоставление режимов и анализ условного числового примера. Предложено правило выбора доли проверяемых результатов, объединяющее лимит ожидаемых потерь, условие неотрицательного прироста чистой приведённой стоимости и доступный фонд рабочего времени. Для заданного соотношения затрат и предотвращаемого ущерба выведен допустимый интервал проверки и условие его существования. Разработан порядок оценки вероятности ошибки и доли предотвращённого ущерба на независимой выборке с учётом неопределённости оценок. В основном сценарии лимит принят равным потерям действующего процесса; при исходных параметрах допустимый режим отсутствует. Повышение лимита рассмотрено отдельно и требует решения уполномоченного владельца риска. Показано, что положительный денежный результат может сочетаться с нехваткой работников для проверки. Механизм обоснован расчётным способом для выделенного класса операций. Его эффективность для управления инновационным проектом в целом ещё не подтверждена эмпирическим исследованием.

items.abstract: This study aimed to (1) examine the levels of work motivation, organizational loyalty, and organizational commitment among personnel of Prince of Songkla University, Trang Campus; (2) compare organizational commitment across personal characteristics; and (3) investigate the influence of work motivation and organizational loyalty on organizational commitment. A quantitative research design was employed, with questionnaire data collected from 125 personnel selected through stratified random sampling. The data were analyzed using the independent-samples t-test, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), and multiple regression analysis. The findings revealed that (1) personnel exhibited high levels of work motivation, organizational loyalty, and organizational commitment, with intrinsic motivation exceeding extrinsic motivation and compensation and benefits yielding the lowest mean score; (2) organizational commitment differed significantly by gender, age, employment type, personnel type, length of service, affiliation, and salary level, with employment type showing the most pronounced difference. Civil servants or personnel with converted status, as well as those with 21 or more years of service, demonstrated the highest level of commitment, whereas revenue-funded or project-based personnel, as well as those with five or fewer years of service, demonstrated the lowest; and (3) both work motivation (β = 0.371) and organizational loyalty (β = 0.525) exerted significant positive effects on organizational commitment at the 0.01 level, jointly accounting for 71.70% of its variance (R² = 0.717), with organizational loyalty emerging as the stronger predictor. These findings suggest that the university should prioritize strengthening organizational loyalty while concurrently improving compensation and benefits, particularly for contract-based personnel and those with shorter tenure.

items.title: (No) Separation of Concerns: Philosophical Concerns about Agent Ethics and Implications for SE Practitioners
items.abstract: The use of AI agents in software engineering (SE) are commonplace, with differing levels of autonomy, a myriad of capabilities, and ability to perform a variety of tasks. Philosophers have begun to examine the ethics of such agents, and SE researchers or practitioners could benefit from them; on the other hand, SE practitioners currently explore most of these concerns through the lens of principlism. We bridge this gap by reviewing the philosophical literature on AI agents indexed in PhilPapers, and translating its ethical concerns into a research agenda for SE researchers and into implications for teams that use coding agents. A systematic mapping study of PhilPapers -- a major philosophy index and open access archive -- yielded 33 peer-reviewed papers by professional philosophers published since 2023. We coded these papers thematically, with cross-disciplinary review of the emerging themes, resulting in eight themes and 85 codes. From these, we derive seven research questions for SE, covering developers' reliance on agents, responsibility for agent-written code, ethical constraints in agent configurations, and benchmark design. For practitioners, we derive five implications: decide which choices an agent must refer to a human, keep agent-written pull requests small enough to review, pair configuration-file instructions with checks, watch for changes to tests, and record who approved what. We argue that ethical concerns cannot be separated from SE concerns into a module of their own: they arise inside code review, configuration, evaluation, and requirements work, and addressing them requires cross-disciplinary work.

items.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Multi-Agent Systems Through a Layered Taxonomy Spanning Science, Engineering, and Applications
items.abstract: Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant architectural paradigm for applied AI, yet deploying them effectively requires bridging scientific understanding of agent coordination with engineering constraints and real-world application demands. This survey presents a unified perspective on the multi-agent AI landscape, synthesizing research across the science of how multiple LLM-driven agents coordinate, the engineering of systems that implement that coordination under production constraints, and the application-level evidence of where such systems deliver measurable value. We introduce a layered taxonomy of multi-agent capabilities, spanning Agent Primitives, Coordination, Communication, Intelligence, and Assurance. We then organize 13 functionalities into 8 key concepts derived inductively from the literature, situated within the layered taxonomy of multi-agent capabilities: (Agent specialization, Orchestration patterns, Decision making, Context engineering, Learning, Evaluation, Tracing & Monitoring, and Security & Safety). For each concept, we trace its intellectual origins, survey current scientific findings, examine engineering design patterns, and ground the discussion in enterprise deployments. We motivate multi-agent architectures through an analysis of single-agent limitations (including context saturation, instruction-following degradation, tool selection noise, and limited modularity) while acknowledging that multi-agent decomposition is not universally superior and introduces its own coordination overhead. We identify principled criteria for when multi-agent coordination is justified over single-agent designs, and examine the responsible AI mechanisms necessary for trustworthy operation at scale. We conclude by outlining directions for future research on open challenges, including evaluation difficulty, cost efficiency, emergent security threats, and governance in a rapidly shifting regulatory landscape.

items.title: A Discussion of Community Diplomacy among Heterogeneous Human–AI Collectives
items.abstract: Who should represent a human–AI community depends on its institutional strategy, the proposed act, and the relations through which authority and practical competence are constituted. This paper connects representative selection, collective-position formation, external recognition, and continuing cooperation. It distinguishes constituencies, appointing bodies, holders, resource controllers, counterparties, and affected parties. A standard categorical pullback describes the conjunction of internal appointment and counterpart acceptance where required. Constructed constitutional histories and a standard judgment-aggregation countercase show how similar capabilities and consistent constituent judgments can support different arrangements and public positions. Agents can recognize attributed histories and selected norm derivations, acknowledge a documented contribution, and undertake bounded obligations through an authorized procedure. An archive encounter preserves plural origin narratives while enabling a restricted review and an agent’s liaison appointment. A standard proof-path functor describes replay under accepted translations and premises. Historical truth, situated interpretation, normative standing, and an operative undertaking retain distinct grounds. A further case negotiates incompatible public-audit and source-confidentiality requirements through a scoped accommodation. Its continuation examines registry standard changes, authority to hear objections, disconnection, and succession after exit. Recognition and interoperability thus become relations whose governing interfaces can themselves be contested and revised. The analysis also develops commitment stages, resource reservation, revocation, and archival continuity. Primary engagement with representation, configurable governance, recognition theory, electronic institutions, AI delegation, institutional economics, and standards supplies antecedents. Selected empirical studies locate federated governance frictions and asymmetries within their observed settings. The proposed contribution connects collective voice and continuing reception to heterogeneous epistemic means, distributed controllers, and plural institutions. Conditional mathematical results and finite diagnostics retain their assumptions. Observation and later implementation can assess effects on cooperation, human presence, answerability, and opportunities to revise a relation.

items.title: A Discussion of Responsibility, Standing, and Remedy in Human–AI Communities
items.abstract: Human–AI communities combine brief contributions with continuing projects, shared resources, and consequential undertakings. This paper develops remedial continuity as a way to investigate whether a live claim can reach an authorized and practically meaningful response through institutional change. A comparative jurisprudential inquiry connects relational powers, plural normative orders, collective identity, resource rights, evidence, and access to remedy. Selected primary legal and philosophical sources retain their jurisdictions, statuses, and argumentative scopes. Developed cases distinguish an operational actor from a represented party, operation-specific responsibility from a whole delegation chain, and claim recognition from the beneficiary and authority of a response. Human interests, protective conduct rules, and possible direct AI claims require their respective grounds. A typed route diagnostic identifies the relevant party, competent forum, lawfully usable evidence, and feasible response. Standard conditional constructions examine transition, archival answerability, jointly feasible schedules, and irreversible response order. A sustained cross-community conflict shows how historical recognition and a successful bounded agreement can coexist with contested permissions, excluded agency questions, external claims, and funding gaps. Further comparisons follow exploitation allegations, translated complaints, shared control, community splits, and continuing duties through changing operational carriers. The framework preserves configurable constitutions and context-sensitive strategies while making the effects of those choices assessable. Its contribution is a specified comparative research architecture and conditional diagnostics; implemented inquiry, independent normative criticism, and jurisdiction-specific analysis are needed to evaluate particular arrangements.

items.title: A Risk-Adaptive Trust and Safety Governance Framework for AI-Enabled Online Platforms: An Advanced Methodology for Identifying, Measuring, and Mitigating Digital Harm
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into online platforms has created significant trust and safety challenges because AI systems can generate, amplify and distribute digital harms across different platform functions and stages of the AI lifecycle.This study develops a Risk-Adaptive Trust and Safety Governance Framework for AI-Enabled Online Platforms as a methodology for identifying, measuring, prioritising and mitigating digital harm.A systematic literature review and conceptual framework-development design was adopted.Relevant literature published between 2017 and 2024 was examined across major academic databases and authoritative sources, with attention given to AI-enabled digital harms, their determinants, risk assessment, risk classification, platform governance and mitigation strategies.The analysis indicates that AI-enabled digital harm is not limited to technical errors or harmful content but can emerge through data practices, model design, deployment conditions, algorithmic ranking, recommendation, moderation, personalisation and organisational decisions.The study further establishes that effective risk assessment requires multidimensional indicators that consider likelihood, severity, exposure, scale, vulnerability and contextual conditions rather than relying exclusively on technical performance measures.On this basis, the proposed framework connects five interrelated processes: identification of digital harm, examination of its determinants, measurement of risk, classification and prioritisation, and proportionate trust and safety mitigation.The framework adopts a continuous feedback approach in which risk assessment informs intervention and the outcomes of intervention generate evidence for subsequent reassessment.The study concludes that effective AI platform governance requires adaptive, evidence-based and accountable trust and safety mechanisms capable of responding to changing technologies, user behaviour and emerging forms of digital harm.

items.title: A Study on Feedback Engagement of College English Learners under a Human-AI Collaborative Writing Feedback Model
items.abstract: This study explores how 50 first-year English majors respond to a DeepSeek-based human-AI collaborative English writing feedback model. Data are collected through a background questionnaire, a questionnaire on feedback engagement, as well as students’ initial and revised writing drafts. The results reveal that students generally have a positive attitude towards this feedback model, but the three-dimensional engagement is uneven. While the cognitive engagement reaches the highest level, behavioral engagement is the lowest. This lack of sufficient behavioral commitment has been confirmed in a moderate level of feedback adoption rate shown in students’ actual writing. In addition, students’ revisions are mostly made on surface language problems, and less demanding revision suggestions are implemented. It is therefore concluded that, when designing a human-AI collaborative writing feedback model, teachers can regulate the feedback content and interaction mechanism with AI, so as to promote students’ overall feedback engagement.

items.title: Adaptive Support Has Limits: AI-Supported Learning Assistance and the Risk of Never-Skilling
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled adaptivity promises to make academic learning support scalable across levels of achievement. This conceptual paper argues that educational value depends on what assistance leaves learners to do, rather than on its quantity alone. It develops a theory-informed synthesis of the assistance dilemma, cognitive load theory, self-regulated learning, and constructive alignment; it does not report a systematic review or an original empirical study. Adaptivity oriented towards challenge preserves a defined competence threshold while varying instructional scaffolding. Relief becomes problematic when it substitutes for the cognitive and metacognitive operations through which that competence is acquired. Randomised studies show that unrestricted and pedagogically constrained AI assistance can produce different learning outcomes, but these findings do not establish a long-term developmental deficit. Building on the term Never-Skilling introduced in medical education, the paper proposes a mechanism in which repeated substitution reduces opportunities for practice and may alter learners’ willingness to invest effort. Never-Skilling is defined as persistently lower acquisition of a specified competence than under comparable instruction that preserves learner processing, assessed after AI support is withdrawn. It differs from deskilling, which concerns loss of established competence, and from cognitive offloading, a strategy that can support or impede learning. Assessment arrangements may conceal an acquisition deficit when AI-generated products count as evidence of independent competence. A further possibility, that assessment standards themselves adjust under institutional pressure, is presented as a separate, unconfirmed hypothesis. The paper specifies measurable constructs and four testable hypotheses concerning unsupported transfer, learner processing, assessment validity, and standards drift. Its design recommendation is to adapt routes to a clearly defined standard while checking retention and transfer without substitutive support. These propositions require longitudinal and context-sensitive validation; they do not imply that AI assistance necessarily prevents learning or that an initial deficit is irreversible.

items.title: Agentic AI for Autonomous Detection and Resolution of Hold Transactions in Integrated Multi-Vendor Hospital Pharmacy Systems
items.abstract: This paper presents an agentic artificial intelligence framework that detects, diagnoses and resolves hold transactions, which are stuck or failed transactions, in integrated hospital pharmacy environments. Large health systems often run order entry, medication processing, billing, stock and inventory, laboratory, blood bank and automated dispensing software from different vendors, and holds arise at the interfaces where no single vendor sees the whole transaction. Analysts resolve holds manually today, so backlogs build up and stock records drift from physical reality. The research problem is how to automate the repetitive part of this work without weakening audit, inventory accuracy or patient safety. Using a design science approach, the paper develops a taxonomy of five hold causes, a five agent architecture based on a monitor, analyze, plan, execute and knowledge control loop, a tiered autonomy policy with approval gated reprocessing, and an artificial intelligence governance model. A 30 day simulation with 20 replications and a sensitivity analysis evaluate the design. Under stated assumptions, about 82 percent of holds are resolved automatically and mean handling time falls from about 43 to 11 minutes, but the human escalation queue stays bounded only above a break even of about 80 percent automatic resolution. The work indicates that governed agentic automation is a promising option for multivendor hospital pharmacy operations, provided that automatic resolution and false fix rates are confirmed through the staged pilot protocol proposed here.

items.title: Agentic AI in education: design logic, evidence quality, and theoretical foundations
items.abstract: Introduction Agentic artificial intelligence systems in education represent a qualitative departure from traditional educational technology. Unlike reactive tools requiring continuous human direction, agentic AI monitors learner states, initiates interventions without requests, and pursues pedagogical objectives independently. Yet this technical sophistication has outpaced theoretical development, leaving fundamental questions unaddressed: How does agent autonomy affect learner agency? When does proactive support enhance versus undermine self-directed learning? What theories adequately address systems demonstrating independent goal pursuit? Methods This study analyzes recent agentic AI research using the ADO-TCM (Antecedents-Decisions-Outcomes-Theories-Contexts-Methods) framework, which traces design logic from problem identification through decisions to outcomes while assessing theoretical grounding, contextual boundaries, and methodological rigor. Following PRISMA guidelines, three researchers independently coded the titles and abstracts of 170 primary studies, achieving substantial agreement. Results As reported in titles and abstracts, the field is characterized by theoretical absence rather than diversity: the vast majority of papers engage no learning theory and invoke AI capabilities as rationale without engaging learning sciences foundations. Alongside this absence, most abstracts do not report whether agents operate autonomously or under supervision, papers addressing multiple problems more often bundle several pedagogical roles in one agent, and most abstracts report outcomes without comparison groups. Because coding was based on titles and abstracts, these gaps describe reported information and require full-text examination before they can be attributed to the underlying research. Discussion Existing theories (e.g., zone of proximal development, cognitive load theory, self-determination theory, activity theory) inadequately address agentic AI's autonomous characteristics. Scaffolding anticipation, autonomy load, and distributed autonomy are offered as conceptual propositions for extending them. We propose theoretical directions, evidence standards, and equity-centered principles to advance agentic AI research from atheoretical demonstration toward theoretically grounded, methodologically rigorous, and equitably distributed practice.

items.title: AGI and Education 5.0: A Systematic Review of AGI-Driven Sustainable Education Across the Learning Lifespan
items.abstract: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is increasingly envisioned as a transformative force in education, yet research on AGI-driven education remains fragmented across educational stages and rarely incorporates sustainability into system design and evaluation. This systematic review examines how AGI and large language model (LLM)/generative AI technologies reshape education across the learning lifespan and how sustainability can be embedded in AGI-powered education. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2015 and 2026, using keyword groups related to general intelligence, education, and sustainability. After screening, 85 peer-reviewed studies were included and synthesized through narrative synthesis. Given that full AGI remains unrealized, current LLM and generative AI systems are treated as emergent approximations of AGI’s educational potential. We develop an organizing framework that maps AGI’s transformative roles, key mechanisms, and sustainability implications across early childhood, K–12, higher education, and lifelong learning. The review identifies four emerging application scenarios and introduces a multidimensional sustainability lens encompassing cognitive, economic, social, and ethical–environmental dimensions, extending evaluation beyond conventional academic performance indicators. It also highlights persistent technical, social, and ethical challenges. By integrating stage-specific transformations with a lifespan and sustainability perspective, this review provides a reference and research agenda for the responsible and sustainable integration of AGI into Education 5.0.

items.title: Agricultural operations centers and data-driven management in the sugarcane sector: foundations for the design of operational procedures and their impacts
items.abstract: The mechanization of sugarcane harvesting and the spread of digital technologies in the field have increased the amount of data available on machines, trucks and agricultural operations, which has favored the creation of agricultural operations centers dedicated to real-time monitoring of field crews. This article, based on a narrative review of scientific, technical and regulatory literature, discusses the foundations that should guide the design and use of operational procedures in these centers, as well as their expected impacts. The analysis brings together contributions from digital agriculture, agricultural machinery engineering, harvest and transport logistics, cognitive ergonomics, decision theory and studies on workplace monitoring. The results indicate that the value of an operations center depends less on the amount of data collected and more on the quality of data recording, the definition of indicators consistent with the actual losses of the system, clarity about who decides and within what time frame, the handling of alarms and the integration of analysis routines into the continuous improvement cycle. It is concluded that well-structured procedures can convert connectivity and telemetry into operational, safety and sustainability gains, provided they are accompanied by data governance, transparency with workers and systematic evaluation of results.

items.title: AI-Assisted Desk Verification of Sentinel-2 Training Samples for Coastal Land Cover Mapping
items.abstract: Supervised land cover mapping of a historical baseline needs reference labels that can no longer be collected in the field. This study documents and evaluates a desk verification workflow that produced Sentinel-2 training samples for a 2019–2020 baseline map of the Lima Puluh coastal landscape, Batu Bara, North Sumatra (about 24,300 ha), where oil palm, paddy, mangrove and aquaculture ponds meet. Candidate points were generated in Google Earth Engine from rule-based frames in two rounds. A multimodal large language model proposed a label and a structured note for each candidate from very-high-resolution basemap chips and Sentinel-2 2019–2020 chips, and the researcher reviewed every proposal. Of 1,114 candidates, 1,024 were reviewed; 450 were confirmed, 364 rejected and 210 left uncertain. A 100 m within-class spacing rule gave 434 training points in seven classes. Frame precision ranged from 0% for index-only water masks to 98% for map-anchored settlement frames. In the priority review of 64 uncertain water and pond points, 58 were excluded, mainly because of mixed land–water pixels, ambiguous fallow plots and water that appeared after 2019; the researcher overrode 1 of 64 proposals. Targeted additions of oil palm and coastal paddy points raised spatially cross-validated kappa from 0.823 to 0.860 and, on a blind validation sample of 300 points, overall accuracy from 0.850 to 0.873 and paddy producer’s accuracy from 0.709 to 0.846. AI-assisted desk verification can supply auditable training data when field access is impossible, provided that a human decides every label and accuracy is estimated independently.

items.title: AI-assisted virtual patient simulation and communication self-efficacy in healthcare professions students: a randomized pilot study
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare systems is transforming not only clinical practice but also the educational pathways preparing future healthcare professionals. This pilot study examines the pedagogical use of AI-assisted conversational simulation in healthcare professions education, comparing AI-based virtual patient interaction with traditional role-play. A randomized parallel-group pilot study with a post-test-only design involved 56 students enrolled in the Master's Degree Program in Diagnostic Technical Healthcare Professions at the University of Foggia. Participants were randomly assigned, through stratified randomization with permuted blocks, to AI-assisted communication training (Group A, n = 28) or traditional role-play with human facilitators (Group B, n = 28) in 1:1 allocation. The 20-hour educational intervention integrated Medical Humanities, healthcare communication, experiential learning, and simulation-based education; Group A trained with a publicly available custom GPT virtual patient using the voice mode of ChatGPT Plus. Communication self-efficacy (SE-12), the primary outcome, was significantly higher in Group A (mean difference 5.74, 95% CI 3.08–8.40; Cohen's d = 1.18, 95% CI 0.60–1.76), an effect that persisted after adjusting for prior AI experience. Communication apprehension (PRCA-24), the secondary outcome, did not differ significantly between groups, either overall or on any of the four subscales. These preliminary findings suggest that AI-assisted conversational simulation may usefully complement traditional communication training and contribute to the broader debate on digital literacy in health professions curricula. The post-test-only design, the single assessment at 7 days, and the use of a non-validated Italian translation of the SE-12 limit inference about causality and durability.

items.title: AI-Driven Digital Transformation: Reconfiguring the Organization While Remaining Responsive to Emergent Risk
items.abstract: A challenge for organizations is that AI-driven digital transformation introduces both unseen and unprecedented risk. From a systems perspective, such risk develops between formal constraints and situated practice; organizational members must interpret AI outputs in context and determine whether to accept, modify, or override them. Risk becomes more apparent when outputs are unexpected, system behavior is difficult to explain, or experience with existing tools raises concerns. Such interactions among organizational members and AI systems serve as a form of distributed sensing, whereby indications of risk are detected and interpreted jointly and iteratively rather than through centralized monitoring. The growing prevalence of generative and agentic AI makes this capacity relevant to organizations, as members initiate actions with AI systems under conditions that cannot be fully specified in advance. AI-driven digital transformation therefore calls for organizations to maintain ongoing interpretation and adjustment, enabling them to balance control with coordinated, adaptive action while remaining responsive to emergent risks.

items.title: AI-Driven Emotion Recognition and Decision-Making in Mental Health: Ethical and Psychological Implications for Early Detection and Human-Computer Interaction
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being integrated across various fields. AI advancements have catalyzed a paradigm shift in psychological assessment and intervention, aiming to rapidly transform how mental health and psychological imbalance are assessed, monitored, and treated. In this research, we examine the role of AI in the early detection of affective and cognitive disorders, with a focus on depression, anxiety, and stress-related psychopathologies using emotion recognition technologies and predictive modeling. We explore how affective computing techniques such as facial expression analysis, speech recognition, and natural language processing are integrated within digital mental health platforms for efficient therapeutic alliance, accurate clinical decision-making, and boosted user engagement. In addition, this research investigates the effects of human-computer interaction in an AI-powered mental health context, addressing constructs such as user trust, engagement, and cognitive reliance on autonomous systems. A critical analysis of ethical and governance factors demonstrated several pitfalls that hinder AI-driven mental health adoption. These include algorithm opacity and bias, non-compliance with regulatory frameworks and data protection policies, and inequitable access to existing platforms. The interdisciplinary synthesis employed in this study provides evidence-based insight with strategic recommendations for developing, deploying, and regulating AI-driven mental health solutions in healthcare systems.

It becomes clear from the literature review that there is at least some directevidence of utility-based or feedback-based recommendations for health insurance plans, whereasthere are many machine learning and deep learning studies that deal with cost, claim, fraud or crossselling but not with plan selection. items.title: AI-Generated Code Issues: A Taxonomy from Repository Histories, AI Conversations, and Developer Interviews
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate source code, yet the quality issues in such code remain only partially understood. Understanding these issues can help developers adapt quality assurance practices, such as code review and testing, to better detect problems that may be more common in AI-generated than in human-written code. We study how quality issues in AI-generated code manifest in real software development activities through a mixed-method empirical study that draws on evidence from three complementary sources. First, we mine GitHub commits whose messages explicitly attribute a fix to a problem in AI-generated code, and we manually inspect the 914 matched commits to remove false positives and classify the quality issue being corrected. Second, we collect developers' shared conversations with AI tools, identify conversations including source code and textual signals of model mistakes, and manually analyze 299 of them to classify the underlying quality issue. Third, we interview 20 practitioners and researchers who use AI coding tools to enrich and validate the obtained catalog of quality issues. From these analyses, we derive a taxonomy of 87 types of developer-attributed quality issues in AI-generated code, going beyond functional bugs. Our findings contribute an empirically grounded taxonomy and implications for the design and evaluation of AI coding assistants and agents.

items.title: AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality?
items.abstract: Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. Yet, across conversational settings, discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives. As generative AI agents increasingly participate alongside humans, hybrid human-AI conversations present a new opportunity to address these challenges. We investigate whether AI agents can serve as catalysts for human interaction, improving conversational engagement and broadening collective discourse. We develop a framework for introducing generic and persona-conditioned AI agents into evolving discussions and evaluate it through two complementary studies. First, using agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, we find that AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human conversations, but substantially less semantically diverse. Persona conditioning produces more human-like contributions and narrows this diversity gap, while increasing the representation of underrepresented personas can shift which perspectives emerge without necessarily increasing overall diversity. Second, we conduct a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine discussion threads, comparing human-only conversations with those involving generic or persona-conditioned AI agents. We find that AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by human participants, even though the AI agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity. These findings suggest that the value of hybrid human-AI conversations lies not simply in the content AI agents generate, but also in their potential to stimulate more responsive and diverse interactions among humans.

items.title: AI-supported digital infrastructures in human health chemical risk assessment: recommendations from a joint VHP4Safety/ONTOX workshop
items.abstract: Chemical risk assessment is undergoing a fundamental transition driven by the need for human-relevant, mechanistically informed, and animal-free approaches. Digital infrastructures that integrate New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), including computational models and emerging artificial intelligence (AI) tools, are increasingly considered drivers of this transition. However, their regulatory uptake depends on several factors, including trust, transparency, scientific validity, and the sustainability of the infrastructures. This paper summarises the outcomes from a multi-stakeholder expert workshop, jointly organised by the European Centre for Ecotoxicology and Toxicology of Chemicals (ECETOC), the VHP4Safety project, and the ONTOX project, focusing on the application of AI-supported digital infrastructures in human health risk assessment of chemicals. The workshop explored technical, regulatory, and governance challenges associated with the integration of AI-supported NAMs into regulatory workflows. This was achieved through demonstrations of two recently developed platforms, the Virtual Human Platform (VHP) and Ontology-driven Probabilistic Risk Assessment (OPRA). Key insights highlight that transparency, traceability and explainability tailored to user needs are necessary for adoption and regulatory acceptance, as well as sustained engagement with regulators. Participants emphasised the importance of platform interoperability, and the need for targeted training for end users. Furthermore, long-term sustainability of digital infrastructures emerged as a critical concern, requiring distinct governance beyond project-based funding. Based on these insights, actionable recommendations for the design, implementation, and governance of AI-supported digital infrastructures to enable regulatory uptake of NAMs are reported. These recommendations are intended to inform developers, regulators and stakeholders advancing next-generation chemical risk assessment across regulatory domains.

items.title: AI, Bias, and Inclusion: A Two-Phase Mixed-Methods Study of Gender Bias, Awareness, and Trust in Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are widespread across fields such as healthcare, finance, employment, and criminal justice, with a substantial impact on the lives of individuals and society. However, it has been established that AI systems perpetuate existing social inequalities, particularly through biases that are not easily discernible. Such biases are embedded in the technical and social structures of artificial intelligence systems, making them difficult to detect. These biases challenge the concept of Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (EDI), which recognizes diversity as the acknowledgment of individual differences, equity as fairness and equal access, and inclusion as the value placed on all participants. This study argues that fairness in artificial intelligence systems cannot be achieved by focusing solely on their technical aspects, necessitating a holistic approach. This study employs a two-phase mixed-methods design. Phase 1 applies computational content analysis to 360 occupational narratives generated by ChatGPT across four countries (Canada, Germany, India, and Bangladesh) using gender-neutral prompts to examine whether professions are predominantly associated with one gender and whether these patterns remain consistent across regions. Phase 2 examines the extent to which students recognize potential bias in AI, their trust in AI for consequential decision-making, and how these perceptions relate to themes in EDI and AI ethics scholarship. By combining output-level bias analysis with user perception data, this study identifies the empirical foundations necessary for future EDI-AI co-design frameworks, outlining the sociotechnical dimensions that such frameworks must address to be effective.

items.title: Algorithmic Management in Australian Workplaces: A Study on Transparency, Accountability and Worker Protection in AI-Driven Employment Decisions
items.abstract: AI systems are widely used in recruitment screening, job allocation, performance evaluation, remuneration decisions, promotion and dismissal. Compared with traditional human management, algorithmic management can improve information-processing efficiency and assist employers in making complex workplace decisions. This article employs doctrinal legal analysis to examine the regulation of AI-driven employment decisions under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), anti-discrimination law and the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). Drawing on Mobley v Workday Inc and Houston Federation of Teachers v Houston Independent School District, it identifies the practical limitations of the existing legal framework. The analysis finds that Australian law provides partial protection, but remains fragmented and reactive. Workers generally obtain remedies only after an adverse decision has occurred, while the current framework lacks adequate pre-deployment disclosure, risk assessment, independent auditing and meaningful human review. It recommends prior disclosure, individualised reasons for adverse decisions, restrictions on solely automated decisions, clear employer accountability, algorithmic impact assessments, periodic independent audits and worker participation. These reforms would not prohibit workplace AI; rather, they would establish a more appropriate balance between technological efficiency, fairness, accountability and worker protection.

items.title: An Agent-Based Modeling Framework Integrating Social Behavior into GIS Digital Twins for Smart Disaster Management
items.abstract: Natural hazards are not purely physical phenomena but coupled human–environment systems in which consequences are shaped by behavioral, infrastructural, and institutional dynamics interacting with physical processes. While current Geographic Information System (GIS)-based digital twins, enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI), have advanced our capacity to monitor and predict physical hazard dynamics, they leave the social and behavioral dimensions of disaster largely unrepresented. This gap in situational intelligence constitutes a critical failure in smart disaster management, such as evacuation gridlock, warning non-compliance, and cascading infrastructure failures triggered by human decisions. This chapter discusses Cognitive Spatial Intelligence Systems (CSIS) as a new framework that addresses this gap by integrating five intelligence layers: Spatial Intelligence (GIS), System Intelligence (digital twins), Predictive Intelligence (AI and machine learning), Social Behavioral Intelligence (agent-based modeling, ABM), and Decision Intelligence (Environmental Decision Support Tools, EDST). Each layer answers a distinct scientific question that the others cannot resolve: where, what is happening, what will happen, how will people and systems respond, and what should we do. The chapter traces the evolution of spatial intelligence from static cartography through digital twins to CSIS; argues for ABM as the behavioral simulation engine for coupled human–environment hazard systems; and grounds the framework in the California wildfire system as a case study. This framework lets emergency managers anticipate behavioral responses, including evacuation decisions, traffic bottlenecks, warning compliance, and physical hazard forecasts. Integrating social simulation into operational digital twins will shift disaster management from reactive response toward active, behavior-aware decision support.

items.title: An Empirical Study on the Use Behavior for Healthcare Professionals to Utilize ChatGPT to Support Clinical Work
items.abstract: In the medical field, healthcare professionals often need to diagnose and treat patients based on their descriptions and disease characteristics. During this process, ChatGPT can serve as an auxiliary tool, offering professional advice and supporting clinical decisions. After treating patients, healthcare professionals typically need to provide follow-up health education, such as explaining diagnoses, prescriptions, treatment plans, and necessary precautions. ChatGPT can handle these tasks on their behalf. Utilizing the UTAUT2 model framework, this study incorporates additional variables such as trust, privacy risks, salary, and education level to understand the factors influencing healthcare professionals' willingness to use ChatGPT for job assistance. Surveys were conducted among healthcare professionals serving in medical institutions at the regional level and above, and data was analyzed using descriptive statistics and structural equation modeling. The study results can serve as a reference for healthcare institutions planning to implement relevant information technologies.

items.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action
items.abstract: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%). For crawler tarpit output, adding a period to the end of each paragraph increases the curation survival rate from 16.4% to 91.9%. We also find that crawler tarpit and data-poisoning output has already entered Common Crawl, a widely used public web archive, and that crawler tarpit output has also entered FineWeb, a released pretraining dataset. We hope our study can facilitate a better understanding of online conflict over generative AI and its implications for content moderation and AI training.

items.title: Applications of large language models in creativity and knowledge generation: A scoping review
items.abstract: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are being explored for scientific ideation, writing, and learning. This scoping review examines creativity and knowledge generation in medical and healthcare-related research and education, with particular attention to LLMs and generative AI. Methods The review followed the PRISMA-ScR reporting framework. Searches of PubMed, Google Scholar, and Dimensions on 7 May 2025 identified 381 records; Google Scholar retrieval was limited to the first 200 results sorted by relevance. After duplicate removal and screening, 99 studies were included and charted. No formal critical appraisal or meta-analysis was undertaken. Results and conclusions The included literature addresses scientific research support (n = 39), creativity in education (n = 23), pedagogical and technological innovation (n = 23), ethical and epistemological concerns (n = 12), and human–AI collaboration (n = 2). The included studies span healthcare-specific and general scientific or educational literature, as well as different AI technologies and evidence types. General AI readiness, self-reported innovativeness, assisted writing, and model performance are distinct from measured effects of LLM use on scientific creativity. Findings from other disciplines provide context but cannot establish medical benefit. Reviews and conceptual or theoretical papers accounted for 63 of the 99 studies, and experimental studies for 16.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Journalistic Practice in Nigeria: Examining Professional Competence, Ethical Challenges and News Credibility
items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and journalistic practice in Nigeria, focusing on professional competence, ethical challenges and journalists’ perceptions of news credibility. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among practising journalists across print, broadcast and digital media organisations. Data from 392 respondents were analysed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha reliability analysis, Pearson’s product-moment correlation and multiple regression. AI applications were most commonly used for grammar checking and editing (77.0%), content generation (73.0%) and automated transcription (69.1%). Respondents reported moderate-to-high perceived professional competence (M = 3.48), alongside comparatively lower scores for identifying inaccuracies and independently verifying AI-generated information. Ethical challenges were rated highly (M = 4.04), particularly inadequate organisational guidelines, misinformation risks and excessive dependence on AI. Journalists’ perceived news credibility score was also high (M = 4.08), reflecting strong support for human editorial supervision, independent fact-checking and transparency. The regression model showed professional competence as a positive predictor and ethical challenges as a negative predictor of journalists’ perceived news credibility. The study concludes that responsible AI integration requires continuous professional training, institutional ethical guidelines and strengthened editorial oversight.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Strategic Decision-Making in SMEs
items.abstract: Purpose. This review examines the factors shaping artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and how AI use may influence strategic decision-making. Design/methodology/approach. The article presents a focused integrative review of peer-reviewed research and selected empirical or practice-based evidence sources, centred on work published from 2015 to 2025 and informed by foundational adoption and decision-making theories. Eleven sources form the core evidence base. Because dated search logs and record-level screening counts were not preserved, the review is not presented as a systematic review or as exhaustive. Findings. SME adoption is shaped by owner-manager knowledge and attitudes, organisational readiness—including data and skills—and environmental pressures. Available evidence supports AI as an aid to decision preparation more strongly than as a substitute for human strategic judgement. Productivity and decision-quality effects vary by task, expertise and trust; much generative-AI evidence comes from settings outside SMEs, so proposed SME-level outcomes require direct testing. Originality/value. The review connects SME technology-adoption research with human–AI decision-making. It develops a framework linking adoption conditions, adoption depth, decision processes and outcomes, and advances six propositions for future empirical research.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Business Management: A Framework For AI-Assisted Decision-Making
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can support business managers by forecasting demand, identifying operational exceptions, andsummarizing information. Its contribution depends on how firms incorporate these outputs into decisions and assess theconsequences. This article develops a framework for AI-assisted decision-making through a conceptual synthesis of selected research on organizational decision structures, AI capabilities, and workplace productivity. The framework comprises four stages: defining the business decision and its baseline, assigning decision authority, piloting AI in the workflow, and evaluating business outcomes before expanding its use. An illustrative inventory replenishment case demonstrates how forecast accuracy, managerial overrides, and service levels can be assessed together. The case shows why an improvement in forecast accuracy can leave ordering decisions unchanged and why lower stockout rates should be evaluated alongside inventory costs. The article’s contribution is to connect AI implementation to decision accountability and measurable operational outcomes. The framework requires empirical validation across business functions and organizational settings.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in IT Project Management: A Critical Analysis of Benefits, Challenges, and Risk Management Strategies
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing information technology (IT) project management with intelligent automation, predictive analytics, and data-driven project decisions over project lifecycles. Nevertheless, even though AI may enhance operational efficiency, the implementation of this technology has witnessed technological, organizational, and ethical issues, which can cripple the impact of a project. This paper has critically analyzed the advantages and limitations of the use of AI in IT project management with a particular interest in the implications of AI for technical project managers and performance in organizations. An ordered literature review and thematic synthesis of the related publications on IEEE Xplore are suggested to analyze the existing evidence on AI-based scheduling, resource allocation, risk prediction, and project governance. Special consideration is made for relationships such as technological capabilities, organizational readiness, data quality, and human oversight. The article further addresses the issue of whether the enhancement of operational efficiency will inevitably lead to the sustainability of project success, in particular, when the complexity of integration, bias in algorithms, the problem of cybersecurity, and labour constraints are not well managed. The research seeks to bridge these dimensions in order to come up with an evidence-based framework, which would direct responsible AI adoption within the management of IT projects. It is expected to provide a better understanding of the conditions in which AI may be used to assist in the delivery of a project, without jeopardizing managerial responsibility, transparency, and organizational control.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: Methodologies, Clinical Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated as a means of improving the collection, interpretation, and use of health information. Applications range from image based diagnosis and clinical risk prediction to workflow support, drug discovery, remote monitoring, and population health. This narrative review examines the methodological foundations of AI in medicine, summarizes representative clinical applications, and critically evaluates the conditions required for safe and equitable implementation. It distinguishes conventional machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and generative AI, while emphasizing that the suitability of a method depends on the clinical question, data structure, intended user, and consequences of error. Evidence from retinal imaging, dermatology, breast cancer screening, and health system prediction illustrates both the promise and the limitations of algorithmic systems. Across these domains, high performance in retrospective datasets does not automatically demonstrate improved patient outcomes. External validation, calibration, prospective evaluation, workflow integration, monitoring for data drift, and clear accountability are essential. Ethical concerns include privacy, informed consent, bias, unequal access, automation bias, explainability, and the environmental and institutional costs of deployment. International guidance and reporting standards, including WHO guidance, CONSORT AI, SPIRIT AI, DECIDE AI, and TRIPOD+AI, provide useful structures for governance and transparent research. The review concludes that AI should be treated as a sociotechnical clinical intervention rather than a stand alone software product. Its most defensible role is to augment appropriately trained healthcare professionals, improve access and consistency where validated, and support rather than replace clinical judgment and patient centred care.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy of College Students and Their Ethical Utilization
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities for learning in higher education while raising concerns about academic integrity, privacy, bias, and misinformation. This study examined AI literacy and ethical AI utilization among second-year Bachelor of Secondary Education major in Science students at City College of Calapan and investigated their relationship as a basis for proposing an institutional framework. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was employed, involving 43 respondents purposively selected from a population of 48 students. Data were analyzed using weighted means and Pearson’s correlation coefficient. Findings revealed high AI literacy in technical knowledge (M = 2.77) and prompting (M = 2.58), but low literacy in critical evaluation (M = 2.42). Ethical utilization was rated low across academic integrity compliance (M = 1.82), ethical awareness and data privacy (M = 2.17), and bias and misinformation mitigation (M = 2.43). The overall relationship between AI literacy and ethical utilization was not statistically significant (r = −0.135, p = 0.389). However, technical knowledge demonstrated a significant moderate negative relationship with bias and misinformation mitigation (r = −0.458, p = 0.002). These findings suggest that technical competence alone does not necessarily translate into responsible AI use. Accordingly, an Institutional Artificial Intelligence Program and Policy Framework adapted from Bilgin’s responsible AI framework was proposed. It comprises AI literacy development, AI utilization policy, AI detection and support tools, monitoring and support, and ethical awareness. The framework emphasizes responsible, ethical, and competent AI utilization through institutional guidance, critical evaluation, academic accountability, and continuing development initiatives for students and faculty.

items.title: Artificial intelligence training labour and the training economy: How generative models reconfigure value extraction in the digital economy
items.abstract: This article theorises an emergent training economy in which selected forms of human cognitive, evaluative, corrective, annotative and creative activity become inputs into the training, alignment, evaluation, validation or optimisation of generative AI systems. It develops AI training labour as the analytical category naming these contributions across contracted, precarious and unrecognised arrangements, with particular attention to weakly compensated or institutionally obscured activity. Drawing on digital labour theory, platform political economy and critical data studies, the article argues that generative AI reconfigures platform capitalism by creating a productive route through which selected digital participation can contribute to model development alongside advertising, subscription, cloud and rent-based accumulation. It distinguishes three evidentiary statuses: documented, where technical incorporation is publicly established; inferred, where a credible incorporation pathway exists but actual use is not independently confirmed; and governance risk, where disclosure is insufficient to determine whether incorporation occurs. These are analytically separate from labour status, which ranges from contracted and paid to unpaid and unrecognised. items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Green Recruitment Practices and Their Impact on Employee Engagement and Retention: An Empirical Study of Sustainable Human Resource Management
items.abstract: This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Green Recruitment Practices and its impact on employee engagement and retention. Integrating AI with Green Human Resource Management enables organizations to digitize recruitment, reduce paper consumption, minimize unnecessary travel, improve candidate screening and matching, and communicate sustainability-oriented employment values. AI can support candidate sourcing, resume screening, virtual assessments, interview scheduling, candidate communication and recruitment analytics. However, organizations must also address concerns relating to fairness, transparency, privacy, algorithmic bias and excessive automation. Following the structure of the supplied model paper, the present study adopts a quantitative approach using a structured questionnaire and an illustrative sample of 300 respondents. Frequency analysis, Chi-square, ANOVA, correlation, and multiple regression are used to examine the relationships among AI-enabled green recruitment practices, employee engagement, and retention. The illustrative findings indicate significant associations between AI-enabled green recruitment and employee engagement and retention intention. Fairness and transparency, perceived environmental responsibility and employee engagement also emerge as important factors associated with retention. The study recommends human oversight, transparent AI governance, monitoring of algorithmic bias, responsible data management, digital, paperless recruitment, and alignment between recruitment promises and actual green organizational practices. The study concludes that AI can strengthen Green Recruitment Practices and contribute to employee engagement and retention when technological efficiency is combined with authentic sustainability and responsible HR management.

items.title: Artificial intelligence, new product development, and design: Towards a framework for artificial intelligence adoption in innovation research
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasingly central role in organizations’ digital transformation. There is growing scholarly interest in how AI supports innovation, that is, how activities and processes aimed at producing novel ideas, problem solutions or other outputs can be enabled by autonomous machines. This article focuses on the role of AI in new product development (NPD) and aims to develop theoretical insights into how AI is reshaping innovation processes. In a systematic review of 1,192 articles published in business and management journals between 1993 and 2024, we identified 67 relevant to AI, NPD, and design. Through a focus on design activities, choices and results, we analyse how AI has been adopted in NPD processes. We find that AI can help manage design complexity and relax traditional constraints, evidencing an alignment with theoretical frameworks centered on process and methodology; at the same time, current adoption of AI in NPD remains largely focused on the implementation and pursuit of measurable performance outcomes. By integrating our findings with existing innovation and AI literatures, we propose an integrative framework that builds on three pillars—strategic orientation, collaboration architecture, and value optimization—and sheds light on the role of governance as a meta‐level coordination mechanism.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence: Innovative Tools for Idea Registration and Evaluation
items.abstract: Suggestion systems play an important role in encouraging employee participation, improving organizational processes, fostering innovation, and enhancing productivity. However, traditional suggestion systems often face challenges such as the accumulation of unevaluated ideas, repetitive submissions, lengthy evaluation procedures, and a lack of transparent and integrated assessment mechanisms.This presentation explores how artificial intelligence can transform organizational suggestion systems, covering the entire process from idea registration and enrichment to preliminary screening, analysis, and evaluation. It first introduces AI-powered assistants that can convert raw notes and initial ideas into structured proposals, enrich technical and economic information through interactive questioning, identify similar or duplicate submissions, and connect new ideas to the organization's existing knowledge and previous experiences.The presentation then examines the intelligent idea evaluation cycle, including preliminary screening, multi-criteria scoring, impact simulation, and hybrid decision-making. Particular attention is given to AI agents designed to identify similar proposals, analyze supporting documents and evidence, assign preliminary scores based on approved criteria and weights, identify strengths and weaknesses, and flag proposals requiring further technical, financial, or legal assessment by experts.In the practical section, an AI-powered Idea Evaluation Agent is introduced, and its application is demonstrated through the analysis of a sample organizational proposal. The presentation also highlights essential requirements for successful implementation, including data confidentiality, algorithmic transparency, integration with organizational knowledge management systems, and maintaining human oversight in final decision-making.The main objective is to demonstrate how artificial intelligence can transform traditional, administrative suggestion systems into intelligent, transparent, and effective mechanisms that convert employees' ideas into organizational value and innovation.

items.title: Ask or Act: A Calibrated-Confidence Framework for Risk-Aware Navigation Under Uncertain Human Intent
items.abstract: Mobile robots that share space with people must decide within seconds whether a pedestrian is about to cross their path, and confidence-based rules that ask the person only when unsure promise to combine safety with efficiency. Such rules are only as safe as their predicted probabilities, yet calibration is usually fitted and evaluated over all available samples, most of which come from moments far from any decision, and its closed-loop effect under distribution shift is rarely tested. We present Ask or Act, a framework in which a robot predicts the probability that a pedestrian will cross, calibrates it, and at a decision deadline yields, proceeds or asks. We propose decision-aware calibration, fitted only on the window in which the robot decides, and evaluate it with a TurtleBot3 in ROS~2 and Gazebo, using eight scripted pedestrian behaviors with known intent under five distribution shifts and a pre-specified analysis plan on held-out scenarios. Under degraded tracking, raw and conventionally recalibrated confidence led to collisions in 34.5% and 15.5% of crossing encounters, against 1.3% with decision-aware recalibration, which remained the safer method for all five predictors trained with different seeds (1.3-10.5% against 5.5-15.8%). Under nominal conditions it asked 16% fewer questions than always asking, within a pre-set non-inferiority margin. Offline results agreed with Gazebo in 97.5% of paired episodes, and the pipeline ran on the robot's onboard computer in about per step. For robots that act on predicted probabilities, calibration should be fitted and evaluated where decisions are made.

items.title: Auditing the Judge: Human-Derived Bias Discovery, Quantification, and Mitigation in LLM Judges
items.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators in evaluation and training pipelines, their judgements are often affected by systematic biases that conflict with human preferences. Although prior work has identified various biases and proposed methods for detecting and mitigating them, less attention has been paid to using human preferences to inform bias identification and mitigation. Moreover, these approaches rely heavily on pre-discovered bias lists, overlook bias strength, and depend on costly interventions. In this work, we propose HUB-J, an integrated framework based on human-derived bias factors that detects, quantifies, and mitigates biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems. Our approach leverages human-LLM judgement disagreement cases to automatically discover interpretable bias factors, and utilizes agreement cases to quantify bias strength through controlled input modifications and resulting shifts in model decisions. Finally, building on these quantified biases, we introduce a lightweight, training-free regression-based mitigation strategy that estimates the influence of each bias factor on model judgments and corrects bias-influenced decisions by removing its estimated effect. Empirical results show that HUB-J uncovers both known and novel bias factors, reveals meaningful differences in model susceptibility, and consistently reduces bias-driven decision flips while generalizing across models.
