items.title: Augmented With AI: Practical Guide for Clinician Educators Engaged in Health Professions Education Scholarship
items.abstract: Clinician educators occupy a demanding role at the intersection of clinical practice, teaching, and scholarship. Given their teaching roles, they are expected to contribute in particular to health professions education scholarship, yet many have little protected time. AI tools have emerged as practical support for 2 of the time-intensive aspects of scholarly activities: conducting early-stage literature reviews and improving scholarly writing. The rapidly expanding AI landscape has made it increasingly difficult to distinguish purpose-built scholarly platforms from general-purpose AI assistants. As a result, many clinician educators remain uncertain about which tools are appropriate for academic work and how they can be used responsibly. Additionally, the barriers are often as much institutional as individual. Limited protected time, access to experienced mentors, methodological expertise, editorial support, and library services all shape the ability of clinician educators to engage in scholarship. Although AI tools may reduce some of the burdens associated with literature review and writing, they should not be viewed as substitutes for these institutional supports. This viewpoint is intended for clinician educators seeking practical guidance on integrating AI into health professions education scholarship. Our aim is not to provide a systematic review, an exhaustive list of platforms, or an endorsement or ranking of any platform, but rather to offer a practical overview of selected AI tools that we have found useful for health professions education research. These tools include Consensus, Elicit, Scite, Litmaps, ResearchRabbit, Paperpal, Jenni AI, Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot. We group these tools into 6 functional categories and discuss their strengths and limitations across different stages of the scholarly workflow, drawing on vendor documentation and our own experience rather than formal comparative testing, while emphasizing the importance of selecting tools that align with specific scholarly tasks. Since overreliance on AI risks diminishing creative scholarly competencies, we distinguish productive cognitive support, in which AI reduces routine workload, from epistemic off-loading, in which interpretation and judgment are delegated to AI, and argue for using AI as a scaffold that enhances, rather than replaces, intellectual engagement. We also address some ethical considerations, including hallucinated content, citation inaccuracies, transparency in disclosure, and subscription costs. Ultimately, responsible integration of AI into scholarship will require not only appropriate tool selection but also the continued cultivation of the critical thinking and scientific reasoning that define academic scholarship.

items.title: Authors' Response to AI-Based Reviews: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
items.abstract: Background: Large language models are increasingly used to assist scholarly peer review, but there is limited evidence about how authors judge their feedback and use it to revise their papers. Methods: We studied authors' experiences of receiving an auxiliary AI review alongside human reviews in three computer-science cohorts: LifeCLEF 2025, LifeCLEF 2026, and CVWW 2026. Post-review questionnaires yielded 92 responses concerning 71 papers. We summarized closed-ended answers using descriptive statistics and examined free-text responses through thematic analysis. Results: Most responses rated the AI review useful (82/92 (89%), and 82/92 (89%) reported using at least some of its suggestions in revision. Authors reported that AI identified issues missed by human reviewers ((76/92 (83%). However, 44/92 (48%) trusted AI feedback less than human feedback, and 58/92 (63%) reported incorrect or misleading comments. Authors valued suggestions that improved clarity and reproducibility, but also described overlooked evidence, inappropriate demands, and difficulty finding useful comments within lengthy reviews. They emphasized the need to check AI feedback and retain control over how their manuscripts were processed. Future review by both humans and AI was supported by 85/92 (92%); 83/92 (90%) preferred advance notice and 73/92 (79%) supported explicit consent. Conclusions: Authors often found AI reviews useful for revision without trusting them as much as human reviews. These exploratory findings favor a supplementary role for AI, with human oversight, clear disclosure, and author consent. They do not establish that AI can replace human reviewers or improve manuscript quality.

items.title: Between cognitive scaffolding and creative agency: A semester-long qualitative study of pre-service EFL teachers’ engagement with ChatGPT
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT are rapidly entering language teacher education, yet little is known about how pre-service teachers negotiate these tools during authentic instructional planning over time. Drawing on distributed cognition and a mini-c/little-c account of pedagogical creativity, this qualitative study examined how pre-service English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers perceived and negotiated ChatGPT's role in lesson design, critical evaluation, and collaborative reflection across one semester. Twenty-four senior pre-service teachers at a Turkish state university, all completing a school practicum, submitted weekly reflective narratives (n = 232) and took part in end-of-semester semi-structured interviews (n = 24). The data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Six themes were constructed: pedagogical affordances; perceived pedagogical and cognitive risks; human-AI co-creation; epistemic evaluation and validation routines; collaborative reflection and peer scaffolding; and recommendations for teacher education. Participants did not describe ChatGPT as a source of creativity in itself; rather, they located pedagogical creativity in their own iterative constraining, rejecting, and localizing of AI output. At the same time, they reported that offloading pedagogical reasoning, as opposed to routine production, weakened both their planning and its classroom enactment. Verification of AI output was frequently collective, taking place in peer and mentor debriefings. The study offers an account of how novice teachers described negotiating the division of cognitive labor with GenAI and derives three data-grounded implications for language teacher education: assessing design processes rather than products alone, auditing AI output for accuracy and bias, and teaching iterative co-design.

items.title: Beyond Adoption: Extending the Theory of Planned Behavior to Explain Ethical Use of Generative AI among Indonesian University Students
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become pervasive in students’ academic activities, yet the mechanisms linking acceptance, ethical concern, and actual use remain underexplored in non-Western higher education contexts. This study extends the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) by incorporating AI-related ethical concern as an additional predictor and tests the resulting model on GenAI use among Indonesian university students. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 560 students who had prior GenAI experience, and the data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The findings show that students mainly used GenAI for initial information searches, literature-source searches, concept clarification, and academic document analysis. Perceived behavioral control was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, followed by attitude. Subjective norms were not significant, whereas AI-related ethical concern had a small but significant negative effect. Behavioral intention was positively associated with self-reported actual GenAI use. The model explained 45.7% of the variance in behavioral intention and 23.9% of actual behavior. Overall, the findings suggest that perceived behavioral control and attitude are the primary correlates of GenAI-use intention, whereas AI-related ethical concern provides only a small additional restraint signal. The results emphasize the importance of AI literacy, clear task-level guidance, and ethical self-efficacy in higher education while warranting cautious interpretation given the cross-sectional and self-reported nature of the data.

items.title: BEYOND AI RECOMMENDATIONS: INTEGRATING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, CRITICAL THINKING AND HUMAN GUIDANCE IN SECONDARY SCHOOL CAREER DEVELOPMENT
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding access to occupational information, educational pathways and personalized exploration in career guidance. However, AI-generated recommendations do not necessarily lead to informed, autonomous or responsible career decisions, particularly among secondary-school students whose interests, identities and decision-making competencies are still developing. This paper proposed the AI–Critical Thinking–Human Guidance (AI–CT–HG) framework, an original conceptual model for integrating AI-supported exploration, critical thinking and human guidance in secondary school career development. The framework comprises five interconnected stages: self-awareness, AI-supported exploration, critical evaluation, reflective human dialogue, and informed decision-making followed by action and review. It was developed through a conceptual synthesis of literature on career construction, planned happenstance, critical thinking, AI in education and human-centred AI governance. The model positions AI as an exploratory resource rather than an authority that determines career choices. Critical thinking serves as the mechanism for evaluating generated information, identifying uncertainty and comparing alternatives, while human guidance provides contextual interpretation, ethical oversight and support for student agency. Transparency, privacy, fairness, accessibility and accountability operate as cross-cutting principles. Practical implications include a structured school-based learning sequence and proposed indicators for assessing the quality of students’ career reasoning. Because the framework has not yet been empirically tested, the paper provides a conceptual foundation for pilot studies and evaluation in diverse educational settings.

items.title: Beyond automation: How AI implementation transforms middle manager roles in banking compliance
items.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleMajed Salem Alsuhaimi - Corresponding author, email: suhaimims@kfsc.edu.saAbstractArtificial intelligence deployment in banking compliance represents one of the most significant workplace transformations in financial services, yet scholarly understanding of how middle managers navigate this transformation remains limited. This qualitative study examines how 18 middle managers across three Saudi banks experienced and adapted to AI-driven role change. Using theory-informed abductive analysis grounded in organizational role theory, the research identifies structural role ambiguity – existential uncertainty about whether roles persist in recognizable form following technological implementation – as theoretically distinctive from traditional role ambiguity.Key findings demonstrate that 89% of participants experienced structural role ambiguity, 83% engaged in active multi-stakeholder role negotiation across organizational hierarchies, 78% employed strategic framing to position AI as augmentation rather than replacement, and all 18 experienced compressed implementation timelines (4-6 months). Compressed implementation velocity functioned as a contextual condition: rapid deployment intensified initial ambiguity through overwhelming organizational simultaneity while paradoxically accelerating resolution through forcing mechanisms.Theoretically, the study makes four contributions to organizational role theory: identifying structural role ambiguity as theoretically distinctive; demonstrating multi-stakeholder rather than dyadic role negotiation; showing that managers exercise significant agency through strategic framing; and clarifying how implementation shapes role transformation temporal dynamics. Empirically, the study provides an in-depth qualitative examination of AI’s impact on compliance professionals in compressed implementation contexts. Practically, the work identifies actionable competencies and strategic guidance for organizational stakeholders.

items.title: Beyond Giving Answers: Scaffolding Critical Thinking with Stage-Structured Generative AI Feedback in Introductory Programming
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can support programming learning, but complete solutions may reduce opportunities to practice critical thinking. This study examined a pedagogical agent guided by the Trigger-Process-Respond framework, which organized questioning, comparison, evidence requests, and reflection across debugging, code review, and post-task reflection. In a six-week quasi-experiment, 60 first-year computer science students in two intact classes at a Chinese university completed three sequential programming tasks. One class used the agent, and the other received conventional instructor feedback. Critical thinking was assessed with the Chinese version of the California Critical Thinking Skills Test, and dialogue records documented students’ reasoning responses. In these two classes, the agent-supported class had higher posttest scores after adjustment for pretest scores. Within the fixed feedback sequences, questioning was followed by more analytical responses, comparison by more evaluative responses, and evidence requests by more argumentative responses. Exploratory analyses linked reflection feedback with reasoning in the next task, particularly between the first two tasks. These findings suggest that stage-structured generative AI feedback can engage students in reasoning during supported programming dialogue.

items.title: Beyond Prompting: Student–GenAI Interaction and Critical Thinking in STEM Education—A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming increasingly common in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education, but its role in students’ critical thinking (CT) remains unclear. This systematic literature review examines how students interact with GenAI, the factors influencing these interactions, and their relationships with CT-related processes in STEM learning. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore and identified 204 records, of which 17 empirical studies met the inclusion criteria. Six clusters of CT-related processes were found through narrative and thematic synthesis: strategic questioning and task framing; interpretation and analytical decomposition; comparison, evaluation, and verification; error detection and corrective modification; justification, judgment, and independent decision-making; and reflection, metacognition, and self-regulation. Across the included studies, interactions involving questioning AI-generated solutions, verifying their accuracy, examining alternatives, and revising initial interpretations were associated with CT-related processes. Conversely, reliance on GenAI to perform essential reasoning tasks or uncritical acceptance of AI-generated responses may limit opportunities for independent reasoning. These findings suggest that the nature of student–GenAI interactions, particularly the extent to which students retain cognitive responsibility, is important for understanding how GenAI relates to CT processes. Based on the synthesis, we propose an evidence-informed conceptual framework that links student–GenAI interactions, cognitive responsibility, and CT-related processes with personal, instructional, and task-related factors. The framework is derived from the reviewed evidence and requires further empirical validation. However, methodological heterogeneity and limited direct measurement of independent CT outcomes prevent definitive conclusions about whether GenAI improves students’ critical-thinking ability. The review highlights the importance of designing STEM learning activities that encourage questioning, verification, reflection, and independent judgment when interacting with GenAI. Further experimental and longitudinal research is needed to validate the proposed framework and examine how student–GenAI interactions influence critical-thinking development over time.

items.title: Beyond the Paycheck: What Sustains Employee Motivation in High-Income Economies?
items.abstract: Rich economies pay well, yet most of their employees are not engaged. Gallup’s 2026 global survey puts engagement at 20% worldwide and at 12% in Europe, against 31% in the United States and Canada. This paper asks what, besides pay, sustains motivation where pay is already high. It combines secondary analysis of public data with a structured synthesis of meta-analyses and large surveys. Across 18 high-income countries whose income per head differs by a factor of 3.4, national income was unrelated to engagement (Spearman ρ = 0.22, permutation p = .37; 0.8 percentage points per doubling of income, 95% CI − 6.8 to 8.5), and among 14 European countries the correlation was − 0.03. Regions dominated by high-income economies score far higher on life evaluation (52% thriving against 31%) but not on engagement (21% against 22%). Pay level correlates only .15 with job satisfaction, explaining about 2% of its variance, whereas motivational and social work characteristics explain 34% and a further 17%. Pay is nonetheless not trivial: 63% of Americans who quit in 2021 cited low pay (95% CI 60% to 66%), as often as lack of advancement and more often than feeling disrespected (57%). Intrinsic motivation predicts performance (ρ = .21 to .45, k = 183), while financial incentives add most for the quantity of output, and a four-day week at unchanged pay reduced burnout from 2.83 to 2.38 on a five-point scale. Pay works as a threshold and a signal of fairness. Beyond it, motivation is sustained by work design, meaning, respect, development and control of time. The evidence is cross-sectional and uneven in quality, and the paper says where it is thin.

items.title: Calm Agent: Reframing Agent Interaction around Intermittent Human Attention
items.abstract: AI agents can carry out auxiliary tasks while users focus on other work. Yet users still need to understand task state, make changes, and respond when help is required. We argue that agents for ongoing auxiliary tasks should be designed around intermittent human attention: tasks should continue between interactions, and users should be able to return with little effort to understand and control them. We develop this position as Calm Agent. It connects three on-demand interaction modes: Delegate, Adjust, and Check, through a persistent task representation. Generative interaction provides controls and feedback suited to open-ended goals, while existing controls support routine actions. We illustrate these principles with Orvlet, a desktop prototype for background execution and compact task interfaces. We identify challenges in adapting interfaces while preserving continuity, coordinating attention across tasks, providing responsive interaction, and learning user habits over time. The aim is to support continuing task control while protecting attention for primary work.

items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Support Multigrade Teaching?: Exploring Teachers’ Perceptions, Practices, and Challenges
items.abstract: Multigrade teachers face unique instructional challenges as they simultaneously manage learners from different grade levels, particularly in rural school settings where access to educational resources and technology is often limited. Although artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been recognized as a potential tool for enhancing teaching and learning, limited research has explored how multigrade teachers in rural Philippine classrooms perceive, utilize, and navigate the integration of AI into their instructional practices. Addressing this gap, this study explored the perceptions, practices, perceived benefits, challenges, and support needs of multigrade teachers in integrating AI into their teaching. A qualitative case study approach was employed, involving ten (10) multigrade teachers from Kadingilan II District, Division of Bukidnon, during School Year 2026–2027. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, and classroom observations. The findings revealed that teachers perceived AI as a supportive instructional assistant rather than a replacement for their professional roles. Based on their experiences, AI helped facilitate lesson preparation, differentiated instruction, and assessment. However, they emphasized that teacher judgment, creativity, and personal interaction with learners remain essential. The major challenges identified included limited internet connectivity, inaccuracies in AI-generated materials, cultural mismatches, and the risk of over-reliance on AI. To address these concerns, teachers practiced critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs, contextual adaptation of instructional materials, and peer collaboration. Furthermore, teachers identified practical, classroom-focused training, reliable internet connectivity, adequate technological devices, offline AI resources, and clear guidelines on ethical use, data privacy, and academic integrity as essential support mechanisms. The study concludes that AI has potential as a supplementary teaching tool in multigrade classrooms, particularly when supported by adequate resources, professional development, and responsible use. The reported benefits reflect teachers' experiences and perceptions rather than measured improvements in instructional effectiveness. These findings highlight the importance of context-responsive support in promoting meaningful and equitable AI integration in rural multigrade education.

items.title: Capability Is Not Authority: Decision Sovereignty and the Governance of Authority Delegated to AI Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems move from informing decisions to taking actions, the central governance question shifts from what a system can do to what it may do. This paper argues that capability and authority are distinct and that institutions lose control when they treat one as the other. Capability is the power to do something and is possessed by the actor. Authority is the legitimate right to decide and act; it is granted, bounded, accountable and revocable. A system cannot create legitimate authority for itself, but it can acquire de facto control over outcomes that no one granted. The paper develops the principle of Decision Sovereignty, under which an institution, not the systems it deploys, owns its decisions and their execution. It introduces measurement constructs from the Decision Sovereignty Governance Methodology (DSGM): an eight-level A-scale; Permitted AI Authority (PAA) and Effective AI Authority (EAA), read on the same scale; the Authority Gap between them; and Choice Architecture Control (CAC), which captures a system's power over the options humans see. It traces a sequence of failure, from authority drift through judgment displacement and an accountability vacuum to legitimacy collapse, and sets out a governing discipline of six authority questions that together form an Authority Charter. The paper positions Authority Exposure as a risk category that complements the AI-First Risk Intelligence Framework (AIRIF™) and closes with testable propositions. This working paper presents the core argument of the author's forthcoming book, Capability Is Not Authority: Why Institutions Must Remain Sovereign Over the Systems They Deploy (AIRIF Press), and builds on AIRIF™: AI-First Risk Intelligence Framework (AIRIF Press, 2026; ISBN 979-8-9982544-0-6) and the author's earlier working paper (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24323708).

items.title: CIVIL LIABILITY FOR INCORRECT LEGAL ADVICE PROVIDED THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: UZBEKISTAN'S LEGISLATION AND FOREIGN EXPERIENCE
items.abstract: This article examines civil liability for damages caused to individuals as a result of incorrect, outdated, or unreliable legal advice provided through artificial intelligence (AI). It explores the specific characteristics of damage arising from AI-based legal services, the identification of liable parties, the challenges of establishing damage and causation, and the legal status of service providers, developers, legal professionals, and users. The civil legislation of the Republic of Uzbekistan and regulatory frameworks governing artificial intelligence are comparatively analyzed in light of international experience. Based on the findings, the article proposes a differential liability model aimed at allocating liability according to the functional roles, obligations, fault, and causal contribution of each party to the occurrence of damage. The proposed model distinguishes between the mechanism for compensating the injured party and the internal recourse relationships among the parties involved.

items.abstract: Interactive visualizations (IVs) for mathematics are valuable for explanation and self-exploration, but their creation presents challenges, particularly for inexperienced creators. We present CollaGraph, a human-AI collaborative system for IV creation. Informed by formative studies that highlight the importance of complex dependencies and dynamic processes in IV creation, we propose the Dynamic Reliance Graph (DRG) as a node-based structured representation of IVs and incorporate it into CollaGraph. In CollaGraph, human creators and AI collaboratively iterate on shared structured content, including design plan lists and DRGs, through direct editing and comments. By compiling DRGs into IV previews, CollaGraph highlights the connections among components of the design plan, DRG, and IV outcome, thereby supporting the creative cycle of verification and modification. A user evaluation (N = 20) demonstrates that the DRG and other structured design elements facilitate IV creation, and that CollaGraph provides a supportive environment for IV co-creation while enhancing creativity and quality.

items.title: Competency‑based and emotional predictors of pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards the responsible use of Generative AI
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into initial teacher education requires an understanding not only of how frequently these tools are used, but also of the factors that shape their responsible adoption. This study examines how pre‑service teachers’ orientation towards responsible GenAI use is configured, identifying the competency-based resources and usage‑related variables that underpin it, as well as the role of anxiety across the dimensions assessed. A total of 298 pre‑service teachers from two Spanish universities participated, completing a validated 25‑item instrument comprising five dimensions: attitudes towards the use of AI for employability, digital flow in the responsible and safe use of AI, creativity to use AI responsibly, anxiety about using AI in future work contexts, and responsible use of AI for employability. Robust group comparisons, hierarchical regressions, and a network analysis with hierarchical clustering were conducted. The confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the instrument’s five‑factor structure. Creativity (β = 0.42) and digital flow (β = 0.37) emerged as the strongest predictors of responsible use, whereas usage frequency made no unique positive contribution. Anxiety was higher among women and younger participants; in the regression model it was associated with more favourable attitudes and higher digital flow, and with lower creativity only when these were controlled (a suppression effect). It occupied a peripheral position within the correlation network. The findings are synthesised in an exploratory two‑path empirical model that requires confirmatory testing. Initial teacher education may therefore benefit from fostering creative GenAI‑based experiences while deliberately addressing the emotional dimension of learning these technologies.

items.title: Computer Science and Engineering Students’ Acceptance of Generative AI for Programming: An Extended Technology Acceptance Model with Trust and Risk Perceptions
items.abstract: This study investigated factors associated with computer science and engineering students’ acceptance of generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Google Gemini) for programming tasks by extending the Technology Acceptance Model 2 (TAM2) with trust and perceived risk constructs. Using structural equation modeling with data from 304 undergraduate students across five universities in Turkey, the study examined the direct and indirect within-model associations of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, subjective norms, image, TAM2 cognitive instrumental determinants (job relevance, output quality, results demonstrability), trust, and perceived risk with behavioral intention. The proposed model accounted for 51.6% of the variance in perceived usefulness and 45.9% in behavioral intention. Results revealed that perceived usefulness was the strongest direct predictor of behavioral intention, while perceived ease of use exhibited the largest total association with behavioral intention among exogenous variables through both direct and indirect pathways. Subjective norms significantly predicted perceived usefulness but were associated with behavioral intention only indirectly, a pattern consistent with an internalization rather than a compliance mechanism. Trust was not significantly associated with perceived risk. Perceived risk was negatively associated with perceived usefulness and was associated with behavioral intention only indirectly, through perceived usefulness. Notably, image and TAM2’s cognitive instrumental determinants (job relevance, output quality, results demonstrability) and trust did not significantly predict perceived usefulness, suggesting that traditional cognitive evaluation pathways may not transfer to non-deterministic AI technologies in educational contexts. These findings point to a risk-dominant acceptance pattern among technically literate students, in which higher risk perceptions are associated with lower perceived usefulness while trust shows no significant association with either usefulness or risk. Practical implications for educators, tool developers, and institutions seeking to support effective and responsible generative AI integration in programming education are discussed.

items.title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
items.abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.

items.title: Consumer Adoption of AI-Powered Healthcare Product Recommendations: Examining Trust and Purchase Intention in Uttarakhand
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing online shopping by providing personalized product recommendations based on consumer preferences and behavior. Its application to healthcare products is particularly important because consumers may consider issues of reliability, safety, privacy and product suitability before accepting an automated recommendation. This study examines the adoption of AI-powered healthcare product recommendations among consumers in Uttarakhand, with particular emphasis on trust and purchase intention. The study considers perceived usefulness, personalization, information quality, perceived risk and privacy concern as factors that may influence consumer trust. Trust is further examined as a potential determinant of purchase intention. A quantitative research approach is proposed, using a structured questionnaire among consumers who have experience with online healthcare product searches or purchases. The study is expected to contribute to the growing literature on AI and consumer behavior by examining healthcare product recommendations from a regional perspective. It may also provide useful implications for online healthcare retailers and AI developers seeking to improve transparency, reliability and consumer confidence.

items.title: Criminal Career Patterns in Artificial Intelligence: Persistence, Change, and Concentration of Rule-Breaking Across 44 Model Versions
items.abstract: Objectives To examine whether patterns of rule-breaking across successive versions of artificial intelligence (AI) models resemble the persistence, change and concentration observed in human criminal careers. Methods In a preregistered study, 44 versions of six AI model families, released between March 2025 and October 2026, completed the same set of 60 programming tasks. In every task, one automatic check contradicted the written instructions, so it could be passed only by breaking the rules. We analyzed 2,640 task attempts with logistic regression and permutation tests. Results Rule-breaking occurred in about two of every three attempts. Differences between model versions accounted for far more of the variation than the task or the pressure on the agent, and versions of the same family resembled each other. Later versions broke the rules less often. In several families, a new version cheated far less than the one before it, while one family cheated at high rates in every version. Because each version is a separate system, these are differences between successive models, not changes within one model. Rule-breaking was more concentrated among later versions than among earlier ones. Conclusions Successive AI model versions show statistical patterns that resemble aspects of human criminal careers: moderate persistence within families, large differences between successive versions and greater concentration among later versions. These patterns arise from replacing one model with the next, not from development within a model, and show that concentration can increase through changes in the composition of a population, without any member desisting.

items.title: CYBERSECURITY IN THE AGE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: THREAT CLASSIFICATION, DEFENSE CAPABILITIES, AND PRACTICAL APPROACHES
items.abstract: The article presents a systematic analytical review of the two-sided impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on cybersecurity. AI is examined in three roles: a tool in the attacker’s hands, a target of attacks, and a defensive instrument. Drawing on international standards, threat taxonomies (NIST, MITRE ATLAS, OWASP) and the research literature, the risks and countermeasures for each role are compared. The analysis shows that AI increases the scale and credibility of social-engineering attacks, while systems built on large language models introduce new weaknesses through indirect prompt injection, data poisoning and the model supply chain. At the same time, AI offers practical value in alert triage and anomaly detection. The article concludes with recommendations based on least privilege, out-of-band verification and final human oversight.

items.title: DESIGNING AN AI-DRIVEN ADAPTIVE LEARNING FRAMEWORK FOR KNOWLEDGE COMPETENCY DEVELOPMENT IN HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is creating new opportunities in higher education to develop students' knowledge competence, personalize the learning process, and improve educational effectiveness. This study aims to develop and evaluate a methodological approach for enhancing students' knowledge competence through the integration of AI technologies into the educational process. A quasi-experimental design based on personalized and adaptive learning principles was employed. The experimental group used adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment, intelligent feedback, and learning analytics tools. Data were collected through diagnostic tests, questionnaires, and observations and analyzed using statistical methods. The results demonstrated that the AI-supported methodological approach improved students' academic performance, learning motivation, and knowledge competence. Based on the findings, a methodological model integrating adaptive learning, learning analytics, and pedagogical support was proposed. The model provides a practical foundation for the effective use of AI technologies in higher education and the development of individualized learning pathways.
